# Simple Random Walk: A Motivating Example

## A simple model

Suppose that the price of a stock changes by exactly 1 baht at the end of each trading day.

- Increase by 1 baht with probability $p$
- Decrease by 1 baht with probability $q=1-p$

Let $X_n$ be the stock price after $n$ trading days, with

$$
X_0=a.
$$

The process evolves according to

$$
X_n=X_{n-1}+Z_n, \quad \text{where } Z_n=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{with probability }p,\\
-1, & \text{with probability }q.
\end{cases}
$$

This process is called a **simple random walk**.

---

## From random changes to a process

The successive changes are

$$
Z_1,Z_2,\ldots
$$

and therefore

$$
X_n=a+\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i.
$$

The process is defined at discrete times $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ and has a discrete state space.

For a particular sequence of random changes, we obtain one **sample path**:

$$
X_0,X_1,X_2,\ldots
$$

Different random changes produce different sample paths.

---

## Example: One Sample Path

Suppose

$$
X_0=100
$$

and the successive changes are

$$
+1,\quad -1,\quad +1,\quad +1,\quad -1.
$$

The process evolves as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
n & 0&1&2&3&4&5\\
\hline
X_n &100&101&100&101&102&101
\end{array}
$$

---

## Example: One Sample Path

The resulting sample path is

$$
100\rightarrow101\rightarrow100\rightarrow101\rightarrow102\rightarrow101.
$$

> **One process, many possible paths**
>
> The stochastic process describes all possible random evolution.
>
> A **sample path** is one particular realisation of the process.

---

## The Random Changes

Assume that

$$
Z_1,Z_2,\ldots
$$

are independent and identically distributed, with

$$
\Pr(Z_i=1)=p,
\qquad
\Pr(Z_i=-1)=q=1-p.
$$

Each $Z_i$ represents the change in the random walk during one time step.

---

## The Mean and Variance of an Increment

For each increment,

$$
\mathrm{E}[Z_i]
=
p-q
=
2p-1
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Z_i)
=
4pq.
$$

Thus, the expected change in one time step is determined by the difference between the probabilities of moving up and down.

---

## The Symmetric Random Walk

When

$$
p=q=\frac12,
$$

the random walk is called a **symmetric random walk**.

In this case,

$$
\mathrm{E}[Z_i]=0,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Z_i)=1.
$$

There is no preferred direction of movement:

$$
\Pr(Z_i=1)=\Pr(Z_i=-1)=\frac12.
$$

---

## Mean and variance of the random walk

Since

$$
X_n=a+\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i,
$$

we have

$$
\mathrm{E}[X_n]
=a+n(p-q)
$$

and, using independence,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X_n)
=4npq.
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{E}[X_n]=a+n(p-q),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(X_n)=4npq.
}
$$

For a symmetric random walk,

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{E}[X_n]=a,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(X_n)=n.
}
$$

The variance increases with $n$, so uncertainty about the position of the random walk increases over time.

---

## Simulation: one sample path

A simulation makes the idea of a sample path concrete.

For a symmetric random walk starting from $X_0=0$:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| 
set.seed(123)

n <- 100

Z <- sample(
  c(-1, 1),
  size = n,
  replace = TRUE
)

X <- c(0, cumsum(Z))

plot(
  0:n, X,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Time, n",
  ylab = "X_n",
  main = "One Realisation of a Simple Random Walk"
)
```

The resulting graph is **one possible sample path**.

A different sequence of random changes gives a different path.

---

## Simulation: several sample paths

A single path does not show the range of possible behaviour.

We can simulate several independent realisations of the same process:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| 
set.seed(123)

n <- 100
m <- 10

X <- matrix(0, nrow = n + 1, ncol = m)

for (j in 1:m) {
  Z <- sample(
    c(-1, 1),
    size = n,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  X[, j] <- c(0, cumsum(Z))
}

matplot(
  0:n, X,
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  xlab = "Time, n",
  ylab = "X_n",
  main = "Ten Realisations of a Simple Random Walk"
)
```

Each line is a different realisation of the **same stochastic process**.

All paths start from

$$
X_0=0,
$$

but they evolve differently because the random changes are different.

---

## What does the simulation show?

For the symmetric random walk:

* Some paths move above zero.
* Some paths move below zero.
* Some paths return to zero several times.
* The paths become more dispersed as $n$ increases.

This reflects

$$
\mathrm{E}[X_n]=0,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(X_n)=n.
$$

The simulation gives a visual interpretation of these mathematical quantities.

---

## When $p\neq q$

Suppose

$$
p=0.6,
\qquad
q=0.4.
$$

Then

$$
\mathrm{E}[Z_i]=p-q=0.2.
$$

Starting from $X_0=0$,

$$
\mathrm{E}[X_n]=0.2n.
$$

Thus, the random walk has a positive average direction.

A typical collection of paths tends to move upward as time increases, although an individual path can still move downward for several consecutive steps.

---


## A Probability Involving Several Time Points

Suppose

$$
X_0=100.
$$

Consider

$$
\Pr(X_2=98,X_5=99\mid X_0=100).
$$

First, consider the state at time $2$.

To have $X_2=98,$ the first two changes must both be $-1$.

Therefore,

$$
\Pr(X_2=98\mid X_0=100)=q^2.
$$

---

## From $X_2=98$ to $X_5=99$

Starting from $X_2=98,$ we need to reach $X_5=99$ in three steps.

The required net change is

$$
99-98=1.
$$

Therefore, among the three changes, we need:

- two upward steps;
- one downward step.

---

## Completing the Calculation

There are

$$
{3\choose2}=3
$$

possible orders for the two upward steps.

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X_2=98,X_5=99\mid X_0=100)\\
&=q^2
\left[
{3\choose2}p^2q
\right]=\boxed{3p^2q^3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The calculation separates the path into two parts:

$$
100\longrightarrow98
\quad\text{and}\quad
98\longrightarrow99.
$$

---

## Distribution after $n$ steps

Let

* $A$ = number of upward steps;
* $B$ = number of downward steps.

Then

$$
A+B=n \quad \text{ and }\quad X_n=a+A-B.
$$


Thus, the distribution of $X_n$ can be obtained from a binomial distribution. For example, when $X_0=0$ and $n=2m$,

$$
\Pr(X_{2n}=2m)
={2n\choose n+m}p^{n+m}q^{n-m}.
$$

The random walk can only occupy states with the same parity as the number of steps taken.

---

## A key observation

Suppose that the current state is $X_n=i.$

The next state can only be $i+1 \quad\text{or}\quad i-1.$

Moreover,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i+1\mid X_n=i)=p \quad \text{ and } \quad \Pr(X_{n+1}=i-1\mid X_n=i)=q.
$$


These probabilities do not depend on how the process arrived at $i$.

For example, if $X_n=100,$

then the probability of moving to $101$ is $p$, regardless of the earlier values $X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1}.$

---

## From random walk to Markov chains

The simple random walk has the property

$$
\boxed{
\text{Past}
\longrightarrow
\text{Current state}
\longrightarrow
\text{Future}.
}
$$

Once the current state is known, the past provides no additional information about the next state.

This is the **Markov property**.

The simple random walk is therefore a natural example from which to introduce **discrete-time Markov chains**.

> **Key idea**
>
> The current state contains all the information from the past that is relevant for predicting the next state.



# The Markov Property and Discrete-Time Markov Chains 

## The Markov Property

Consider again the simple random walk. Suppose that

$$
(X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)=(100,99,98,99).
$$

Given $X_3=99$,

$$
\Pr(X_4=100\mid X_3=99)=p, \quad \text{ and } \quad \Pr(X_4=98\mid X_3=99)=q.
$$

The earlier values $X_0,X_1,X_2$ do not affect these probabilities.

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_4=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_3)
=\Pr(X_4=j\mid X_3)
}
$$

The current state contains all the information from the past that is relevant for predicting the next state.

---



## The Markov Property

A discrete-time stochastic process ${X_n:n=0,1,2,\ldots}$ has the **Markov property** if

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i)
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
}
$$

In words:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Past}
\longrightarrow
\text{Current state}
\longrightarrow
\text{Future}
}
$$

Once the current state is known, the past provides no additional information about the next state.

---

## Simple Random Walk

For the simple random walk,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)
=\begin{cases}
p, & j=i+1,\\
q, & j=i-1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

These probabilities depend only on the current state $i$.

Therefore, the simple random walk satisfies the Markov property.

> **Key idea**
>
> The Markov property does not mean that successive states are independent.
>
> $X_{n+1}$ generally depends on $X_n$.
>
> It means that, given $X_n$, the earlier states provide no further information about the future.

---

## Discrete-Time Markov Chain

A **discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC)** is a discrete-time stochastic process that satisfies the Markov property.

Let

$$
{X_n:n=0,1,2,\ldots}
$$

have state space $S$.

The process is a DTMC if

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i,X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0)
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)
}
$$

for all $n\geq0$ and all states for which the conditional probabilities are defined.

The state space $S$ contains all possible values of the process.

---

## Interpreting the Definition 

Compare:

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i) \quad \text{with} \quad \Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_{n-1},X_n=i).
$$

For a DTMC, these two probabilities are equal.

Thus, when predicting the next state, we can replace the complete history

$$
X_0,\ldots,X_{n-1},X_n
$$

by the single value $X_n.$

This is the main simplification provided by the Markov property.

---

## Example: No-Claim Discount System

Let $X_n$ denote the NCD level after $n$ policy years, with $S=\{0,1,2\}.$

Suppose:

* a claim-free year moves the policyholder up one level;
* a claim moves the policyholder down one level;
* the boundary levels are retained when the corresponding movement is impossible.

If the probability of a claim-free year is $p$, then, for example,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=2\mid X_n=1)=p, \quad \text{and} \quad \Pr(X_{n+1}=0\mid X_n=1)=1-p.
$$


These probabilities depend only on the current NCD level.

Hence, the NCD system is a DTMC.

---

## Modeling NCD as a Markov Chain

![No-claim discount](../figures/Modeling_NCD_as_Markov_Chain.png){#fig-ncd-markov fig-align="center" width="80%"}



---

## One-Step Transition Probabilities

For a DTMC, define the **one-step transition probability**

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}^{(n,n+1)}
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
}
$$

It is the probability of moving $\boxed{i\longrightarrow j}$ in one time step.

For every current state $i$,

$$
0\leq p_{ij}^{(n,n+1)}\leq1    \quad \text{and} \quad   \boxed{
\sum_{j\in S}p_{ij}^{(n,n+1)}=1.
} 
$$

Each row therefore gives a probability distribution for the next state.

---

## Example: Simple Random Walk

For the simple random walk,

$$
p_{ij}^{(n,n+1)}
=\begin{cases}
p, & j=i+1,\\
q, & j=i-1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

For example,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=6\mid X_n=5)=p \quad \text{and} \quad  \Pr(X_{n+1}=4\mid X_n=5)=q.
$$


The transition probabilities do not depend on $n$.

This leads to the concept of a **time-homogeneous Markov chain**.

---

## Time-Homogeneous Markov Chains

A Markov chain is **time-homogeneous** if its one-step transition probabilities do not depend on time.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)=p_{ij}
}
$$

for all $n$.

The probability of the transition

$$
i\longrightarrow j
$$

is the same whether it occurs in year 1, year 5, or year 20.

If transition probabilities depend on $n$, the chain is **time-inhomogeneous**.

> **Unless stated otherwise, we assume that Markov chains are time-homogeneous.**

---

## Transition Matrix

For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, collect all one-step transition probabilities into a matrix:

$$
\boxed{
P=(p_{ij}),
\qquad
p_{ij}=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
}
$$

For a finite state space $S={1,\ldots,d}$,

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
p_{11}&p_{12}&\cdots&p_{1d}\\
p_{21}&p_{22}&\cdots&p_{2d}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
p_{d1}&p_{d2}&\cdots&p_{dd}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Rows = current state**

**Columns = next state**

---

## Reading a Transition Matrix

The entry $p_{ij}$ means

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
}
$$

For example,

$$
p_{23}
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=3\mid X_n=2).
$$

Every entry satisfies $p_{ij}\geq0,$ and every row satisfies $\boxed{\sum_jp_{ij}=1.}$

A matrix with non-negative entries and row sums equal to 1 is called a **stochastic matrix**.

---

## NCD System: Transition Matrix

For the NCD system with states

$$
S=\{0,1,2\},
$$

suppose that the probability of a claim-free year is $p$.

The transition rules give

$$
\boxed{
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1-p&p&0\\
1-p&0&p\\
0&1-p&p
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$


---

## Transition Matrix for the NCD Model

![Transition matrix for the NCD model](../figures/NCD_Markov_Chain_Model.png){#fig-ncd-matrix fig-align="center" width="80%"}



---

## Health-Sick-Dead Model

Consider a health insurance model with three states: $S=\{H,S,D\},$

where

* $H$ = Healthy, $S$ = Sick, $D$ = Dead.

Suppose

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
p_{HH}&p_{HS}&p_{HD}\\
p_{SH}&p_{SS}&p_{SD}\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For example,

$$
p_{HS}
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=S\mid X_n=H).
$$

Thus, $p_{HS}$ is the probability that a healthy policyholder becomes sick during the next period.

---

## The Healthy-Sick-Dead Markov Model

![Healthy-Sick-Dead Markov Chain](../figures/Healthy-Sick-Dead_Markov_Chain.png){#fig-hsd-chain fig-align="center" width="80%"}



---

## An Absorbing State

The final row of the HSD transition matrix is

$$
(0,0,1).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=D\mid X_n=D)=1.
$$

Once the process enters state $D$, it remains there.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
D\text{ is an absorbing state.}
}
$$

We will study absorbing states and boundaries later in the chapter.

---

## Weather Model

Consider a simple model with three weather states:

$$
S=\{\text{Sunny},\text{Cloudy},\text{Rainy}\}.
$$

A transition matrix might be

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
p_{SS}&p_{SC}&p_{SR}\\
p_{CS}&p_{CC}&p_{CR}\\
p_{RS}&p_{RC}&p_{RR}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For example,

$$
p_{SR}
=\Pr(X_{n+1}=\text{Rainy}\mid X_n=\text{Sunny}).
$$

Each row describes the distribution of tomorrow's weather given today's weather.

---

## Three Applications, One Mathematical Structure

| Application        | State          | Time step       | Markov interpretation                       |
| :----------------- | :------------- | :-------------- | :------------------------------------------ |
| Simple random walk | Position       | One step        | Next position depends on current position   |
| NCD system         | Discount level | One policy year | Next level depends on current level         |
| HSD model          | Health status  | One period      | Next status depends on current status       |
| Weather model      | Weather state  | One day         | Tomorrow's weather depends on today's state |

The applications have different interpretations, but the same mathematical structure:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Current state}
\longrightarrow
\text{probabilistic next state}.
}
$$

---

## The Transition Matrix as a Model

For a time-homogeneous DTMC,

$$
P=(p_{ij})
$$

contains the complete one-step transition behaviour.

Once $P$ is known:

$$
\boxed{
\text{current state}
+
\text{transition matrix}
\longrightarrow
\text{distribution of next state}.
}
$$

For example, if $X_n=i$, the $i$th row of $P$ gives

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i),
\qquad j\in S.
$$

The transition matrix therefore provides the basic computational representation of a DTMC.

---

## From One-Step to Multi-Step Transitions

The transition matrix describes one-step movement:

$$
P
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i).
$$

In many applications, we need probabilities several steps ahead.

For example:

> What is the probability that a policyholder currently at NCD level 1 will be at level 2 three years from now?

This leads to

$$
\boxed{\text{n-step transition probabilities: } P^{(n)} = P^n}
$$


and, in the next stage, to matrix powers such as $P^2,\quad P^3,\quad\ldots,\quad P^n.$

The next section develops this connection.



# Multi-Step Transitions and State Distributions

## From one-step to multi-step transitions

The transition matrix $P$ describes movement over **one time step**.

In many applications, we need probabilities several steps ahead.

For example:

> A policyholder is currently at NCD level $1$. What is the probability of being at level $2$ three years from now?

This is a **three-step transition probability**.

$$
\boxed{
\text{One step: }P
\qquad
\text{Several steps: }P^n
}
$$

---


## $n$-step transition probabilities

For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, define

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}^{(n)}
=\Pr(X_{m+n}=j\mid X_m=i).
}
$$

This is the probability of being in state $j$ **$n$ steps after starting in state $i$**.

Because the chain is time-homogeneous,

$$
p_{ij}^{(n)}
=\Pr(X_n=j\mid X_0=i).
$$

For $n=1$,

$$
p_{ij}^{(1)}
=p_{ij}.
$$

> The superscript $(n)$ indicates the number of transitions. It is **not** a power of $p_{ij}$.

---

## Two-step transitions

Suppose the chain starts in state $i$ and we want $\Pr(X_2=j\mid X_0=i).$

The chain must pass through some intermediate state $k$: $i\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow j.$

For a particular $k$,

$$
\Pr(X_1=k\mid X_0=i)=p_{ik}
$$

and

$$
\Pr(X_2=j\mid X_1=k)=p_{kj}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}^{(2)}
=\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}p_{kj}.
}
$$

We sum over **all possible intermediate states**.

---

## Example: NCD system


$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1-p&p&0\\
1-p&0&p\\
0&1-p&p
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Suppose the current state is $1$. To reach state $2$ after two years, the possible paths are

$$
1\longrightarrow0\longrightarrow2 \quad \text{ and } \quad 1\longrightarrow2\longrightarrow2.
$$


Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{12}^{(2)}
&=p_{10}p_{02}+p_{12}p_{22}\
&=(1-p)(0)+p^2\
&=p^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_{n+2}=2\mid X_n=1)=p^2.
}
$$

---



## Chapman–Kolmogorov equation

Suppose we want to move from state $i$ to state $j$ in $n$ steps.

Choose an intermediate time $l$, where $0<l<n.$

The process must pass through some state $k$ at time $l$:

$$
i
\overset{l}{\longrightarrow}
k
\overset{n-l}{\longrightarrow}
j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}^{(n)}
=\sum_{k\in S}
p_{ik}^{(l)}
p_{kj}^{(n-l)}.
}
$$

This is the **Chapman–Kolmogorov equation**.

> An $n$-step transition can be decomposed into an $l$-step transition followed by an $(n-l)$-step transition.

---

## Decomposing the Chapman-Kolmogorov Equation

![Decomposing the Chapman-Kolmogorov Equation](../figures/Decomposing_the_Chapman-Kolmogorov_Equation.png){#fig-ck-decomposition fig-align="center" width="80%"}


---

## Why does Chapman–Kolmogorov work?

Partition according to the state $X_l$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}^{(n)}
&=
\sum_{k\in S}
\Pr(X_n=j,X_l=k\mid X_0=i)\
&=
\sum_{k\in S}
\Pr(X_n=j\mid X_l=k,X_0=i)
\Pr(X_l=k\mid X_0=i).
\end{aligned}
$$

The Markov property gives

$$
\Pr(X_n=j\mid X_l=k,X_0=i)
=\Pr(X_n=j\mid X_l=k).
$$

Hence,

$$
p_{ij}^{(n)}
=\sum_{k\in S}
p_{ik}^{(l)}
p_{kj}^{(n-l)}.
$$

The intermediate state $k$ is summed over all possible values.

---

## Matrix Representation

Let

$$
P^{(n)}=(p_{ij}^{(n)})
$$

be the matrix of $n$-step transition probabilities.

The Chapman–Kolmogorov equation gives

$$
\boxed{
P^{(n)}
=
P^{(l)}P^{(n-l)}.
}
$$

Thus, an $n$-step transition can be decomposed into an $l$-step transition followed by an $(n-l)$-step transition.

---

## Matrix Powers

Since

$$
P^{(1)}=P,
$$

the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation gives

$$
P^{(2)}=P^2,
\qquad
P^{(3)}=P^3.
$$

Continuing in the same way,

$$
\boxed{
P^{(n)}=P^n.
}
$$

Thus, matrix powers provide the $n$-step transition probabilities.

---

## Matrix Powers and $n$-Step Probabilities

The $(i,j)$ entry of $P^n$ is the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ in $n$ steps:

$$
\boxed{
(P^n)_{ij}
=
p_{ij}^{(n)}
=
\Pr(X_{m+n}=j\mid X_m=i).
}
$$

For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, this probability does not depend on the starting time $m$.

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
P^n
\quad\text{contains all $n$-step transition probabilities.}
}
$$

---

## Matrix powers and paths

Matrix multiplication combines all possible intermediate states.

For example,

$$
(P^2)_{ij}
=\sum_k p_{ik}p_{kj}.
$$

Each term corresponds to a two-step path $i\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow j.$

Similarly,

$$
(P^3)_{ij}
=\sum_{k}\sum_l
p_{ik}p_{kl}p_{lj}.
$$

Each term corresponds to a three-step path.

$$
\boxed{
\text{Matrix powers}
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{all possible paths over several steps}
}
$$

---




## Example: NCD system

Suppose $p=\frac34$ and 

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/4&3/4&0\\
1/4&0&3/4\\
0&1/4&3/4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then

$$
P^3=
\begin{pmatrix}
7/64&21/64&9/16\\
7/64&3/16&45/64\\
1/16&15/64&45/64
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

If the current NCD level is $1$,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+3}=1\mid X_n=1)
=(P^3)_{11} \quad \text{ and } \quad \boxed{
\Pr(X_{n+3}=1\mid X_n=1)
=\frac{3}{16}.
}
$$

---

## From conditional probabilities to distributions

The transition matrix gives probabilities **conditional on the current state**.

We can also ask: What is the distribution of $X_n$?

Let

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(n)}
=\left(
\Pr(X_n=i)
\right)_{i\in S}.
$$

The initial distribution is

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}
=\left(
\Pr(X_0=i)
\right)_{i\in S}.
$$

By the law of total probability,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j)
&=
\sum_{i\in S}
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)
\Pr(X_n=i) =
\sum_{i\in S}
p_{ij}\mu_i^{(n)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Distribution of $X_n$

In matrix notation,

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(n+1)}
=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(n)}P.
}
$$

Repeating this relation gives

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(n)}
=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P^n.
}
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
P
\longrightarrow
P^n
\longrightarrow
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P^n.
}
$$

* $P$ gives one-step transition probabilities.
* $P^n$ gives $n$-step transition probabilities.
* $\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P^n$ gives the distribution of $X_n$.

---

## Conditional versus unconditional probabilities

| Quantity                        | Interpretation         |
| :------------------------------ | :--------------------- |
| $(P^n)_{ij}$                    | $\Pr(X_n=j\mid X_0=i)$ |
| $(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P^n)_j$ | $\Pr(X_n=j)$           |

The first assumes a specified initial state.

The second allows uncertainty about the initial state.

---

## Example: NCD Distribution After Three Years

Suppose

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/4&3/4&0\\
1/4&0&3/4\\
0&1/4&3/4
\end{pmatrix}
$$

and the policyholder starts in state $1$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}
=
(0,1,0).
$$

---

## Example: NCD Distribution After Three Years

After three years,

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(3)}
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P^3.
$$

Using

$$
P^3=
\begin{pmatrix}
7/64&21/64&9/16\\
7/64&3/16&45/64\\
1/16&15/64&45/64
\end{pmatrix},
$$

we obtain

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(3)}
=
\left(
\frac{7}{64},
\frac{3}{16},
\frac{45}{64}
\right).
$$

---

## Example: NCD Distribution After Three Years

Therefore,

$$
\Pr(X_3=0)=\frac{7}{64},
$$

$$
\Pr(X_3=1)=\frac{3}{16},
$$

and

$$
\Pr(X_3=2)=\frac{45}{64}.
$$

As a check,

$$
\frac{7}{64}
+\frac{3}{16}
+\frac{45}{64}
=1.
$$


---

## Joint distributions

Sometimes we need the probability of a **particular sequence of states**:

$$
\Pr(X_0=i_0,X_1=i_1,\ldots,X_n=i_n).
$$

For a time-homogeneous Markov chain with initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\mu}$,

$$
\mu_i=\Pr(X_0=i),
$$

the Markov property gives

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i_n)
=\mu_{i_0}
p_{i_0i_1}
p_{i_1i_2}
\cdots
p_{i_{n-1}i_n}.
}
$$

Thus, the probability of a particular path is the product of:

1. the initial probability;
2. the transition probabilities along the path.

---

## Example: A particular NCD path

Suppose

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/4&3/4&0\\
1/4&0&3/4\\
0&1/4&3/4
\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{ and } \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}=(0.5,0.3,0.2).
$$


Consider the path $2\longrightarrow1\longrightarrow0.$ Then


$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X_0=2,X_1=1,X_2=0)\
&=
\mu_2p_{21}p_{10}\
&=
0.2\left(\frac14\right)\left(\frac14\right)\
&=
\frac1{80}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X_0=2,X_1=1,X_2=0)=\frac1{80}.
}
$$

---

## Future paths

Suppose the current state is known:

$$
X_n=i_n.
$$

For the future path

$$
i_n\longrightarrow i_{n+1}
\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow i_{n+m},
$$

we have

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(
X_{n+1}=i_{n+1},\ldots,X_{n+m}=i_{n+m}
\mid X_n=i_n)
=\prod_{r=n}^{n+m-1}
p_{i_ri_{r+1}}.
}
$$

The initial distribution is no longer needed because the current state is already specified.

---

## Joint probabilities with gaps

The observed states do not have to occur at consecutive times.

Suppose

$$
0\leq n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_k.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X_{n_1}=i_1,\ldots,X_{n_k}=i_k)\
&=
(\boldsymbol{\mu}P^{n_1})*{i_1}
(P^{n_2-n_1})*{i_1i_2}
\cdots
(P^{n_k-n_{k-1}})*{i*{k-1}i_k}.
\end{aligned}
}
$$

The matrix powers automatically account for the unobserved states between the specified times.

---

## Weather Model

Suppose

$$
S=\{R,C,S\},
$$

where

- $R$ = rainy,
- $C$ = cloudy,
- $S$ = sunny.

Suppose the one-day transition matrix is

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.7&0.2&0.1\\
0.75&0.15&0.1\\
0.2&0.4&0.4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

---

## Weather Model: A Joint Probability

Suppose Sunday has distribution

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}
=
\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right).
$$

Consider the event:

- Wednesday is sunny;
- Friday is sunny;
- Saturday is cloudy.

We want to calculate

$$
\Pr(X_3=S,X_5=S,X_6=C).
$$

The states on Thursday are not specified.

---

## Weather Model: Using Transition Probabilities

The probability can be written as

$$
\Pr(X_3=S,X_5=S,X_6=C)
$$

$$
=
(\boldsymbol{\mu}P^3)_S
(P^2)_{SS}
P_{SC}.
$$

Here, $\boldsymbol{\mu}P^3$ gives the distribution on Wednesday, while $P^2$ accounts for the two-day transition from Wednesday to Friday.

---

## Weather Model: Calculation

Using

$$
(\boldsymbol{\mu}P^3)_S=0.148, \quad (P^2)_{SS}=0.22,
$$


and

$$
P_{SC}=0.4,
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X_3=S,X_5=S,X_6=C) =(0.148)(0.22)(0.4) =\boxed{0.013024}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $P^2$ accounts for the unobserved weather on Thursday.


# Random Walks with Absorbing and Reflecting Barriers

## Why Introduce Boundaries?

The simple random walk can move freely through all integer states:

$$
\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots
$$

In applications, the state space may have boundaries.

For example, a gambler's fortune may be restricted to

$$
S=\{0,1,\ldots,N\}.
$$

We must specify what happens when the process reaches a boundary.

Two important possibilities are:

- **absorbing boundary**: the process remains at the boundary;
- **reflecting barrier**: the process can return to the interior.

---

## Random Walk with Absorbing Barriers

Consider

$$
S=\{0,1,\ldots,N\}.
$$

For an interior state $i$,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i+1\mid X_n=i)=p
$$

and

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i-1\mid X_n=i)=q,
$$

where

$$
p+q=1.
$$

Suppose that $0$ and $N$ are absorbing:

$$
p_{00}=1,
\qquad
p_{NN}=1.
$$

Once either boundary is reached, the process remains there.

---

## Absorbing States

A state $i$ is **absorbing** if

$$
\boxed{p_{ii}=1.}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i\mid X_n=i)=1.
$$

Thus, once the chain reaches state $i$, it cannot leave that state.

---

## Absorbing States

Once the chain enters an absorbing state,

$$
X_n=i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X_{n+r}=i,
\qquad r\geq0.
$$

For the bounded random walk,

$$
0
\quad\text{and}\quad
N
$$

are absorbing states.

---

## Transition Matrix with Absorbing Barriers

For

$$
S=\{0,1,\ldots,N\},
$$

the transition matrix has the form

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&\cdots&0&0\\
q&0&p&\cdots&0&0\\
0&q&0&\ddots&0&0\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&0&\ddots&0&p\\
0&0&0&\cdots&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The interior rows describe the ordinary random walk.

The first and last rows describe the absorbing boundaries.

---

## Gambler's Ruin

Interpret $X_n$ as a gambler's fortune.

- The gambler starts with $i$ units.
- A game is won with probability $p$.
- A game is lost with probability $q=1-p$.
- The fortune changes by one unit after each game.
- The game stops when the fortune reaches $0$ or $N$.

Thus,

$$
S=\{0,1,\ldots,N\},
$$

with

$$
0=\text{ruin},
\qquad
N=\text{target fortune}.
$$

Both states are absorbing.

---

## Questions About Absorption

Starting from state $i$, we may ask:

$$
\Pr(\text{eventually reach }N\mid X_0=i)
$$

or

$$
\Pr(\text{eventually reach }0\mid X_0=i).
$$

We may also ask for the expected time until absorption:

$$
\mathrm{E}[\text{time until absorption}\mid X_0=i].
$$

These are **absorption probabilities** and **expected times to absorption**.

We will use **first-step analysis** to answer these questions.

---

## Reflecting Barriers

A boundary does not have to be absorbing.

Suppose $S=\{0,1,\ldots,N\}.$

For interior states,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i+1\mid X_n=i)=p,
$$

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i-1\mid X_n=i)=q.
$$

At the lower boundary $0$, suppose

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=0\mid X_n=0)=\alpha \quad \text{ and } \quad \Pr(X_{n+1}=1\mid X_n=0)=1-\alpha.
$$

The process cannot move to $-1$.

---

## Absorbing versus Reflecting

| Boundary | Behaviour after reaching it |
|:--|:--|
| Absorbing | Remains at the boundary forever |
| Reflecting | Can move back into the state space |

For an absorbing state,

$$
p_{ii}=1.
$$

For a reflecting boundary, this need not be true.

For example,

$$
0\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{or}\quad
0\longrightarrow1.
$$

Thus, the boundary rule must be included in the transition matrix.

---

## Reflecting Lower Barrier

Consider the state space

$$
S=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

For an interior state $i\geq1$,

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i+1\mid X_n=i)=p,
$$

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=i-1\mid X_n=i)=q.
$$

Thus, the usual random-walk transitions apply away from the boundary.

---

## Reflecting Lower Barrier

At the boundary $0$, the process cannot move to $-1$.

Suppose

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=0\mid X_n=0)=\alpha
$$

and

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=1\mid X_n=0)=1-\alpha.
$$

Hence, the process either remains at $0$ or moves back into the state space.

The first row of the transition matrix is therefore different from the interior rows.

---

## Reflecting Lower Barrier: Transition Matrix

The transition matrix begins

$$
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha&1-\alpha&0&0&\cdots\\
q&0&p&0&\cdots\\
0&q&0&p&\cdots\\
0&0&q&0&\ddots\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\ddots
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The first row reflects the boundary condition at $0$.

The interior rows retain the usual random-walk transitions.

The process can return to the interior after reaching the boundary.
